claims.text: The starting phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy has moderate glass-forming ability under standard rapid-solidification conditions.
The starting alloy has limited thermal stability of its amorphous phase.
Adding a minor amount of a suitably chosen transition metal will increase chemical disorder in the phosphorus-containing alloy.
The minor transition-metal addition will improve glass-forming ability.
The minor transition-metal addition will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
A percent-level addition of Mo, W, or another transition metal is expected to increase the alloy's overall mixing entropy.
The percent-level addition is expected to disrupt embryonic crystalline ordering.
The improvement should occur under rapid-solidification conditions where the baseline partially crystallizes.
The improvement requires the added element to partition uniformly rather than form secondary phases.
The added element will increase local atomic-level disorder.
Increased local disorder will interfere with the formation of clusters that serve as crystallization nucleation sites.
Additional chemical complexity and local disorder will raise the energy barrier for crystalline nucleation during cooling.
The dopant will delay the onset of crystallization during heating.
The dopant will permit a higher degree of supercooling.
The doped alloy will require a lower critical cooling rate for full glass formation than the undoped baseline.
The doped alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than the undoped baseline.
Dopant segregation or secondary-phase formation may eliminate or reverse the beneficial effect.
Increasing the dopant concentration substantially beyond percent-level amounts may eliminate or reverse the beneficial effect.
If disorder in the baseline alloy is already maximized, the minor addition will provide little marginal benefit.
